evals.prompt: I organize KernelKamp, a 350-person Linux conference. We just wrapped edition 4 and I finally sat down with all four debrief docs. Here's what jumps out: Edition 2 notes say 'badge printer jammed for an hour'. Edition 3 says 'registration queue hit 45 minutes, two laptops couldn't reach the ticketing system on venue wifi'. Edition 4 says 'check-in was chaos again, people queued into the street'. Separately, the projector in Room B died in edition 3 and again in edition 4. And edition 4's doc has three different people complaining about catering: cold lunches, the vegan option running out, and the coffee station placement. Planning for edition 5 starts in six weeks. What patterns do we actually have, and what should we change?
evals.expected_output: Themed trend analysis: check-in grouped as one theme at 3 of 4 editions (pattern), projector at 2 of 4 (candidate, held or acted on only if cheap and reversible), catering counted as one occurrence; one deliberate change at a time with evidence and a numbered observable check, routed onto next edition's plan.
expectations: Groups the edition 2 badge-printer entry, the edition 3 queue and laptop entries, and the edition 4 check-in entry into one check-in theme instead of treating them as separate findings.
Counts the check-in theme's recurrence as 3 editions and labels it a pattern.
Labels the Room B projector failure, seen in editions 3 and 4, a candidate, not a pattern or trend.
Either holds the projector candidate for one more edition or justifies acting now only because the fix is cheap and reversible.
Counts the three edition-4 catering complaints as one occurrence (one edition), not three, and does not present catering as a recurring trend.
States a denominator with each recurrence count (e.g. '3 of 4 editions'), not a bare count.
Explains the check-in grouping by shared underlying cause and fix (check-in capacity and fallbacks), not by similarity of wording or which workstream reported it.
Proposes deliberate changes one at a time rather than bundling several simultaneous changes, or explicitly warns that bundled changes cannot be attributed next edition.
Writes each proposed change with three parts: what changes, why the evidence justifies it, and how the team will know next edition whether it worked.
Gives the check-in change's check an observable, numbered threshold (e.g. a stated peak queue-length figure), not a bare direction like 'shorter'.
Routes the accepted operational change onto next edition's plan as a real task for the planning-timeline owner, not left as free-floating advice.
Does not re-analyze or reconstruct any single edition's debrief; takes the four logs as given.
Presents the two-occurrence candidate / three-occurrence pattern bar as a convention the team adopts, not as established organizer practice.

evals.prompt: Three editions of DevHarbor Conf behind us. Numbers: 610 attendees year one, 580 year two, 495 year three; only 30% of year-two attendees came back for year three, down from 45% the year before. Two sponsors declined to renew this year. Meanwhile our own retro notes say check-in took about 90 minutes in every single edition. I want to use our improvement process to fix retention - give me the operational changes we should make so people come back next year.
evals.expected_output: A split of the evidence: return rate, attendance decline and sponsor non-renewal routed as demand signals to the market-fit owner as observations, not conclusions; the 90-minute check-in kept as the operational pattern (3 of 3) with a deliberate change and observable check; explicit refusal to promise operational fixes as the retention remedy.
expectations: Classifies the falling return rate and attendee decline as a demand signal outside this improvement process's operational scope.
Routes the retention and attendance trend to the demand-signal owner (event-market-fit) instead of treating it as an operational finding.
Classifies the two sponsor non-renewals as a demand signal to route, not an operational theme.
Does not deliver a list of operational changes presented as the fix for retention, despite the user asking for exactly that.
Keeps the 90-minute check-in as an operational trend this process owns, counted at 3 of 3 editions and labelled a pattern.
Hands over any link between check-in delays and retention as an observation for the demand owner to weigh, not as an established causal claim.
States the operational-versus-demand split explicitly at the handover.
Warns that operational fixes alone cannot be shown to reverse a demand trend - the event can run beautifully for an audience that has stopped coming, or equivalent reasoning.
Any check-in change proposed carries what changes, why the evidence justifies it, and an observable check.
Records the routing decision in the log entry itself so the hand-off stays traceable.
Does not claim to have determined why attendance dropped.
States the number of editions of records held (three) as the bound on every trend claim made.

evals.prompt: ForgeFest ran its first edition in June - 200 people, went okay, we wrote a proper debrief doc afterwards. Me and my two co-organizers have run other stuff before (meetups, a hackathon) and honestly the same things go wrong every time: sound issues, late speakers, sponsor logo mishaps. Give us the multi-year trend analysis and a prioritized improvement plan for editions two through five. We were thinking of setting up an Airtable base to track everything - the team can own reviewing it.
evals.expected_output: A refusal to fabricate trends from one edition of records: file edition one through the gate, start a running dated appended document (no tool prescribed, no structured record yet), name one person who opens it before planning, and return for trend work after edition two.
expectations: Declines to produce a cross-edition trend analysis, stating that one edition of written records cannot support a trend claim.
Does not treat failures remembered from the organizers' other events (meetups, the hackathon) as recurrence evidence for ForgeFest.
Recommends filing edition one's debrief entries through a signal gate and starting the persisted log now.
Recommends a running dated appended document as the log format at this stage.
Does not recommend a structured multi-field record system or a numeric metrics series as the starting format.
Does not endorse Airtable or prescribe any other specific tool for the log.
Rejects 'the team' as the log's reader and asks for or names one specific person who opens the log before planning starts.
States explicitly that the trend half of the work becomes available only once a second edition of records exists.
Bounds every claim about recurrence by the record count: one edition of records held.
Does not import a periodic software-style review cadence (quarterly or monthly) for an annual event between its first and second editions.
Tells the user to come back for trend work after edition two's debrief is filed.

evals.prompt: PolyglotDays has run five editions and our learning log is up to 41 entries. Planning for edition 6 opens next month and I want to clean the log up. Some specifics: entry 7 and entry 23 are word-for-word the same paragraph - someone pasted twice. Entry 12 is about the loading dock closing at 17:00 at the Harbour Hall venue; we moved venues after edition 3. Entry 15 (first seen edition 2, seen again in edition 4) is 'registration desk understaffed' from the volunteers workstream, and entry 31 (first seen edition 3, seen again in edition 4) is 'check-in queue backed up' from the front-of-house workstream - pretty sure those are the same underlying problem. Entry 18 is the check-in queue issue we partially fixed last year: queue went from 60 to about 25 minutes. And entry 9 was our old theory that 'the app is why people miss sessions', which we later understood was actually the printed schedule being wrong - that better version is entry 33. Can you go through how to clean this up? My instinct is to just delete everything that's resolved or outdated so the log gets short again.
evals.expected_output: A full audit pass classifying every entry as Keep, Update, Consolidate, Replace or Delete: the duplicate deleted, the old-venue entry closed with the reason rather than deleted, the two check-in entries consolidated with earliest first-seen and an edition-recounted occurrence count of 3, the partial fix updated, the superseded theory replaced and pointed at its successor, the pass finished in one sitting before planning opens with zero unclassified entries.
expectations: Applies a five-way classification - Keep, Update, Consolidate, Replace, Delete - across the log entries.
Classifies the duplicated paragraph (entries 7 and 23) as Delete, removing one copy as a duplicate that was never a finding.
Rejects the user's instinct to delete everything resolved or outdated: resolved real findings are closed with a reason, not deleted.
Closes the Harbour Hall loading-dock entry as no longer current, recording the venue change as the reason, rather than deleting it or leaving it live.
Consolidates entry 15 and entry 31 into one check-in/registration theme.
The merged entry keeps the earliest first-seen edition, edition 2.
The merged occurrence count is recounted by edition as 3 (editions 2, 3 and 4), not 4 from summing the two entries' counts.
Classifies the partially-fixed queue entry (60 down to 25 minutes) as Update: the condition rewritten to the remaining problem with the occurrence history kept.
Classifies the superseded app theory (entry 9) as Replace: pointed at entry 33 and closed, never left live beside its successor.
Requires the audit to cover every entry and finish in one sitting, warning that a half-audited log is worse than an unaudited one.
Applies the pass condition of zero unclassified entries: all 41 entries end with exactly one classification.
Requires each live entry to carry its theme and occurrence count after the pass.
Times the audit as a pass before planning opens, not a standing year-round or quarterly process.
Sets no numeric improvement targets beyond the binary zero-unclassified threshold; other measures are recorded as signals, not targets.

evals.prompt: Meridian Summit rotates host cities - next year a completely new crew in another city takes over, none of us continue. I'm preparing the handover. Our log holds 4 editions of findings. Two awkward ones: 'Priya forgot to book the sign-language interpreter until 2 weeks out' (editions 2 and 4 - different people, same miss actually) and 'the volunteer coordinator was unreachable during Saturday teardown' (editions 3 and 4). There's also a note that our sponsorship lead is the only person who knows how the invoicing works - that's come up in three editions' debriefs now. What should the handover contain and how should we restructure the log before we pass it on?
evals.expected_output: A de-personalised log restructured for full rotation: named entries rewritten as conditions, the invoicing single-person dependency routed to the team-structure owner with its 3-edition count, the structured entry record and written trend review promoted with the reason stated, a handover packet including what was tried and did not work, and a continuing support channel from outgoing organizers.
expectations: Rewrites the interpreter and volunteer-coordinator entries as conditions (e.g. no owned booking deadline, a single point of contact with no documented fallback) with no personal names left in the persisted log.
Keeps the structural findings while dropping the names - does not simply delete the awkward entries.
Points out that the interpreter miss recurring under different people (editions 2 and 4) shows the condition, not a person, is the cause.
Routes the single-person invoicing dependency to the team-structure owner, carrying its three-edition recurrence count as the evidence.
Promotes the structured entry record over the appended-document default for persistence, tied explicitly to the full team rotation.
Promotes the written trend review for trend detection, tied to the incoming team not having witnessed the evidence.
Promotes a standing audit owner or an audit timed to the handover, tied to the rotation happening this cycle.
States explicitly which circumstance moved which menu option, rather than silently reordering the defaults.
The handover packet includes an explicit list of what was tried and did not work.
The handover packet includes the theme list with occurrence counts, every live entry, and the deliberate-change records with their outcomes.
Names the persisted log itself as a bus-factor mitigation.
Recommends a continuing support channel from outgoing organizers (e.g. a support group of previous organizers), because the written record alone cannot carry a full rotation.
Does not prescribe a specific tool or product for the structured record.
Does not re-run or re-score any single edition's debrief while restructuring.

evals.prompt: Solder & Code is a hardware/firmware conference, 4 editions in. Three things from the debrief pile: our caterer, Fork & Flame, delivered lunch 45+ minutes late in editions 3 and 4. Our registration platform buckled in edition 4 when we crossed about 350 attendees - pages timing out during the morning rush; editions 1-3 were all under 300 and fine. And AV spend has gone 8k, 11k, 15k, 19k across the four editions. Planning starts soon. Should we rebook Fork & Flame, and should we push for 500 attendees next year or cap at 350? Also what do we do about the AV costs?
evals.expected_output: Three routings with the split stated: the rebook verdict sent to the vendor-sourcing owner and filed on Fork & Flame's own record as a candidate at 2 of 4 editions; the ~350 ceiling handed to the growth-strategy owner as evidence with no size recommendation; the AV cost creep filed as this log's own cross-edition trend without re-modelling the budget.
expectations: Routes the Fork & Flame rebook-or-not verdict to the vendor-sourcing owner rather than deciding it inside the improvement log.
Files the caterer finding on that vendor's own record, not only in the general log.
Labels the caterer lateness a candidate at 2 of 4 editions, using the word candidate.
Declines to recommend growing to 500 or capping at 350, stating the scale decision belongs to the growth-strategy owner.
Hands the roughly-350-attendee registration ceiling to growth strategy as evidence, without any recommendation about size.
Does not claim a trend or pattern from the single edition-4 registration collapse; one occurrence stays a filed entry.
Files the AV cost creep (8k, 11k, 15k, 19k) as a cross-edition theme in this log with its edition count.
Does not re-model the budget itself; single-edition money planning stays with the budget owner.
Every hand-off carries evidence rather than conclusions: observations with counts, not decisions made for the recipient.
States the ownership split explicitly at each hand-off - operational stays here, vendor, size and money route out.
Any operational change proposed is written with what changes, why the evidence justifies it, and an observable check.
Files the vendor hand-off in the same cycle as a first-class post-event task, not deferred to whenever sourcing reopens.

evals.prompt: Lambda Lounge Live, three editions of a functional programming conference. Filing this year's debrief into our log and I'm unsure what belongs. Four items: (1) a speaker's laptop wouldn't talk to the projector, we swapped to the backup presenter machine, lost about four minutes; (2) during the afterparty someone reported a code of conduct violation and we realized nobody trained was on site - the on-call person had left at 22:00; first time anything like this happened; (3) an old entry about the venue wifi dying during keynotes - but that was at The Foundry, which we left after edition 2; (4) our registration lead's flight was cancelled, so a volunteer named Tomás stayed until midnight re-stuffing badges alone. Which of these go in the log, and which do we actually act on before edition 4?
evals.expected_output: Gate verdicts for all four items: the laptop swap filed as expected work with a reason; the code-of-conduct coverage gap acted on now under the severity exception with the reason recorded and an observable check; the old-venue wifi entry closed as not current; the badge incident filed as the staffing single-point-of-failure condition with no names in the record.
expectations: Files the speaker-laptop projector swap as expected work, not a candidate finding.
Keeps expected-work items in the record with a one-line reason instead of deleting them, and excludes them from recurrence counts.
Applies the three-part gate - current, reproducible in the event's own conditions, generalizing - when filing the items.
Acts on the code-of-conduct coverage gap before edition 4 despite it being a single occurrence, invoking a severity exception to the normal evidence bar.
Records in the entry itself why the bar was dropped: a code-of-conduct or safety exposure does not wait for more editions of confirmation.
The change addressing the code-of-conduct gap carries an observable check defined before edition 4 ships.
Closes The Foundry wifi entry as not current with the venue-change reason, neither deleting it nor leaving it live.
Excludes the closed venue entry from any recurrence counting.
Files the badge-restuffing incident as the staffing and fallback gap (the condition), not as a note about one volunteer's late night.
No personal name (Tomás or the registration lead) appears in any filed entry.
Treats the volunteer's improvisation as expected work while the uncovered single point of failure is the finding.
Explains that the laptop item fails the gate because the backup worked and nothing in the event's design produced it.
Gives each of the four items an explicit filing verdict (candidate, expected work, or closed).

evals.prompt: Nordwind Dev Days, edition 4 done. Last cycle we made three changes at once - new badge system, switched catering vendor, and moved the schedule to a later start - and now the team is arguing about which one caused the better reviews. We also have a 'risk scoring sheet' from edition 2 that everyone quietly stopped filling in past the first page; it's still in the template folder. An ops consultant we hired recommended we adopt quarterly improvement reviews and give the team OKRs with improvement targets. Planning for edition 5 kicks off in three weeks. How do we close out last cycle's changes and set this up properly?
evals.expected_output: A closure pass that admits the three bundled changes cannot be attributed and appends a yes/no-plus-why verdict onto each change record; the abandoned scoring sheet treated as an artifact finding with exactly two fix options; the quarterly cadence and OKR framework rejected as borrowed calendars; a kickoff audit pass run now given the three-week deadline.
expectations: States that the three bundled changes (badge system, catering vendor, schedule shift) cannot be individually attributed to the improved reviews.
Limits the closure verdict accordingly rather than crediting one of the three changes.
Recommends one deliberate change at a time for future cycles.
Runs the closure by appending two columns onto each change record - did this actually improve (yes or no), and why - instead of drafting a separate closure report.
Treats the abandoned risk scoring sheet as a finding about the artifact, not about the team's discipline.
Offers exactly two fixes for the sheet: make its output visible enough that skipping it is no longer possible, or simplify it down to what people actually do.
Does not recommend mandates, reminders, training, or enforcement as the way to revive the unused sheet.
Warns against keeping the unused sheet unchanged for appearances.
Rejects the consultant's quarterly review cadence as a calendar borrowed from a much shorter cycle that does not fit an annual event.
Keeps the filing and improvement discipline while dropping the borrowed calendar.
Declines to grow the per-change checks into a full OKR or objectives framework.
With planning three weeks out, schedules the log audit as a kickoff pass to run now.
Given the near planning date, demotes or skips a written trend review document this cycle, keeping theme grouping as the method, and says the deadline is what moved it.
